Special Dispatch to THE EVENING STAR.

Rockville, Md., November 21.—This community was shocked on Saturday evening last by nearing of the brutal and indecent assault committed on a five year old daughter of Charles Lochte, a store-keeper at Montrose, a settlement about four miles from here, on the turnpike leading to Washington, by a negro farm hand named Charles Rigney. The fiend got the little girl to go to the barn with him to look up something which he said he had lost. Mr. Lochte was busy at the store at the time, and his first intimation as to the terrible crime that had been committed was in seeing the girl come from the barn, her clothes being literally torn from her. After learning the facts, Mr. Lochte started after the negro. His tracks were found, showing that he had gone into the woods. In a little while he was overtaken and would have been killed on the spot by the enraged father of the child, but he was prevented from doing so by those who had assisted him in the capture. With four other men Mr. Lochte tied and bound the negro securely with a rope, and placing him in a wagon drove him to this place, when he was regularly surrendered to Sheriff Kelchener and by him turned over to Jailor Kingsbury. On the way up from Montrose one of the five tied a rope around the neck of the prisoner. It was with this rope that he was led after he was lifted out of the wagon. It is said that the lynching would have taken place before the jail was reached had not two of the five men indulged a little too freely in cider just before they started from Montrose.

Rigney made a similar attempt on a little girl about a year ago. He left the neighborhood in consequence of it and only recently returned. Prior to that it is charged that he endeavored to get another girl to go into the woods with him. He was seen in jail by THE STAR correspondent this morning. He was hideous enough before, no doubt, but now has a bruised eye and swollen nose, the result of the pounding that Mr. Lochte gave him when he caught him. He denies the crime, but his denial is not given any consideration, for he was seen going to the barn with the child and then caught as he was running away. He said he thought some people would have come to hang him last night, and was extremely glad that no such visit was made him.

There were threats of lynching him heard on Saturday night and again yesterday, but better counsel prevailed until the grand jury has heard the evidence. The grand jury met this morning and is now in session. Several witnesses have been examined. Should they find an indictment for rape, the impression is that the ravisher will be taken out of jail to-night and lynched on the same tree that Diggs, the colored ravisher, was hanged about a year ago. This will save the state expense, as the law hangs all convicted for rape. Should the indictment be for an attempt at rape, he will not be lynched, but he will undoubtedly get the full extent of the law in the penitentiary ten years. It therefore depends entirely on the action of the grand jury whether or not Rigney will see another morning's sunrise. Report comes here that a party is being organized at Montrose to come here to-night. Several have received invitations to "meet at Rockville, on important business." Sheriff Kelchener says he fully expected an attack on the jail last night, but does not apprehend any for to-night, as he thinks the excitement has quieted down. The jailor, to be on the safe side, has taken extra precautions to keep his prisoner. Rigney says he is but nineteen years of age. He looks at least four years older. M. J.

A Revolting Assault Upon a Child.
ROCKVILLE, MD., Nov. 20.—The five year old daughter of Charles Loehle, who resides at Montrose, in Montgomery county, was brutally and indecently assaulted by a colored man named Charles Rigney, who worked on an adjoining farm, on Saturday afternoon. The negro enticed the girl into a stable; the act was discovered soon afterwards and the negro arrested by the girl's father, who would have killed him on the spot had it not been for the interference of others, who assisted in bringing him to the jail here.

There was talk of lynching him last night, and the talk was resumed tonight, but so far nothing have been done in that direction. The grand jury will be in session tomorrow, and the evidence will be heard.
charles-rigney-rockville-1881-11-19.A7: THE MONTROSE, M.D., OUTRAGE CASE.—A special to the Baltimore Sun from Rockville, Md., November 25, says: The grand jury here to-day returned an indictment against Rigney, charging him with an attempt at outrage. His victim is not injured so much as was at first thought, and the chances of his lynching have about passed away. A Brutal Outrage.—It appears that the terrible and swift vengeance which was broken upon the negro Diggs in this county a little over a year ago, has been forgotten or has lost its salutary effect upon a certain class of the colored population, for, on Saturday night our community was startled by a report that a similar crime had been committed at Montrose, a small, scattered village, about two miles from Rockville on the pike leading to Georgetown, but in the main is stripped of the horrid and repulsive features of the Diggs affair. In this instance a little five-year old daughter of Mr. Chas. Lochte being the victim, and Charles Rigney, a colored lad, the culprit.

On the afternoon of the day in question, Mrs. Lochte, while busily engaged in the domestic duties of her household, supposed their little daughter was in the store with its father, and he, that the child was with its mother, but in this they were both mistaken, for the negro had enticed her to the stable by offering her twenty-five cents to accompany him. The little victim was quite a favorite or pet with the frequenters at Mr. Lochte's store, and many a nickle and penny fell into her palm from admiring friends. In her childish and confiding simplicity it was no wonder she accompanied him and was by him brutally assaulted and outraged. The little child, as soon as it could escape the clutches of this fiend, went to the house, where the mother soon discovered the true state of affairs and informed her husband who called the negro out of his store and accused him of the crime, after which he proceeded to give him a severe thrashing, and possibly if some cooler heads had not been present, there would have been a darky funeral in that locality soon after; but the crowd interfered and saved the worthless life of the scoundrel. Rigney was then securely bound, placed in a wagon and brought before Justice Morgan, of this place, who, after hearing the evidence, committed him for the action of the grand jury then in session, who found a bill of attempted rape. In conversation with the physician who attended the little child, we learn that her injuries are not of a serious nature, but this does not lessen the enormity of the crime and the punishment it deserves. The intent of the villain cannot be doubted, and a sure and speedy punishment should follow. The security of female virtue demand it, the morals of every community claim this of the law, and every law-abiding citizen should see that it is enforced; and should moral suasion, law, conscience and common decency fail to prevent a repetition of this kind, there is for criminals of this character a terrible ultimatum held in reserve. There is a limit to all human endurance and patience, and when that point is passed in cases like the present a swift retribution follows the steps of crime.

This creature Rigney, says he is about nineteen years of age, and it is rumored that this is the second offence of this kind in which he was an active participant. If such should prove to be the case we think a jury could do no better service to the community and the culprit in particular than to send him to the penitentiary for a term of eight or ten years. "Out west," it is more than probable the local newspapers would briefly report this case in about the following language: "He was unanimously chosen by a convention of property holders to jump from the tail end of a wagon into the sweet subsequently."

Civil Service Reformers. BOSTON, Nov. 10.—The secretary of the Cambridge Civil Service Reform Association has received a letter from the central committee of the National Civil Service Reform League informing him of a resolve by the committee to send a delegation to wait upon President Arthur soon after the assembling of Congress in regular session, inviting the Cambridge Association to add one more delegate. WASHINGTON December 12, 1907

A WHEELING AUTHOR'S TWO NOVELS.

Specia Correspondence of the Register.

WASHINGTON, December 12.—I met Mr. J. W. St. Clair, the prosecuting attorney of Fayette county, here to-day, and had considerable talk with him concerning the recent miners troubles in the Kanawha section. He is a middle aged, muscular and plucky looking individual, and seems like the right sort of a man to hold his own in a rough community. He said he thought the troubles in his section of the State had been settled for the time being, and had been settled in the only way in which it was possible to settle them. "It had come to be a mere question," he said, "whether the coal operators in the coal valley should control their own property or not; and as the miner's association was so constructed and extended that trespassers could not be punished under the present laws, the only way to get along was to meet

Force With Force

when trespasses were attempted. I advised Wyant, one of the larger operators in the valley, whose employees were about to be interfered with, that if he posted his place and warned the strikers not to come on it, that he would have the right to keep them off, and, if necessary, shoot and drag them off. "Well," said Wyant, "if that is the law, I'll keep 'em off," and getting a box of shotguns he put them in the hands of trusted employees, and has been free from annoyance ever since.

The Faulkners, who have mines in the same neighborhood, pursued the same course and with the same success, and Eugene Dana, who manages the Campbell's creek mines, a little lower down, get along comfortably by exhibiting similar nerve when threatened.

As to the Recent Trouble

at Strain's, he said, the strike was ostensibly made against the railroad in the first instance, the men admitting that the operators could not pay the advance asked without an increase in the price paid for coal by the C. & O. agency. The mine owners used every effort to get an advance, and when they were unsuccessful offered their former miners a chance to go back to work at the old prices before trying the experiment of importing colored miners. The old hands refused to take hold or allow any one else, and got the first set of negroes imported to stop, by threatening their lives if they did not, and offering to take care of them if they did. It was in this part of the transaction that the women figured, assembling at the pitmouth with pans and sticks, their husbands and friends meanwhile congregating in the vicinity to the

Number of Several Hundred.

"You may not think a demonstration by women would amount to much," added St. Clair, "but when you come to tackle a crowd of square-built English and Welsh women, some of whom can whip an ordinary man in a fist-fight without any trouble, it is not so trifling a thing." Anyhow it was enough, aided by the backing at hand, to scare out the new hands, and some of them craw'ed out through the air-course in preference to facing the mob. The next lot brought on were negroes of the same class, and it was a mere question of protecting or abandoning the owners in their right to work them. The strikers, numbering about 400, were waiting for the negroes at the station, and the county officials

Were Powerless

to assert their authority and protect the new hands. The Sheriff, Tyree, is a man of good courage and equal good sense. He knew he could get no pass sufficient to bear him out in the immediate neighborhood. He had the right to call on the nearest organized military company or battalion for assistance without consulting the Governor, but he thought the authority of the Chief Executive would have weight, and the Governor promptly gave him permission to use such authority for the purpose of doing what he had a right to do without it. That was all there was of it. We got two companies on the ground and guarded the negroes from intrusion a couple of days until the strikers saw that they could not intimidate them into leaving and dispersed.

"Isn't there any other way to meet these troubles when they arise?"

"Not at present, and under similar circumstances. We have no proper legislation on the subject of trespass, and you can't very well go back to the common law proceeding on an information before a magistrate. Besides, with the influence of the Miner's Union against you, it is almost impossible to get testimony from witnesses who have full knowledge of facts. You have no idea of the class you have to deal with. There is not so much trouble with the Americans, Irish and negroes, but the English and Welsh contain a good many troublesome characters who work up most of the devilment. If I have received one anonymous letter

Threatening My Life,

I have had 20. The day I shot the negro who was endeavoring to escape, I was threatened by a mob, and at other times I have had to get out shooting irons in order to assert my right to stay where it was my plain duty to be. What is needed to put an end to this state of things, is legislation like that which stopped similar troubles in Pennsylvania. I know there will be some trouble in getting it, because there are always some members who will not act as they know they ought to act, for fear of losing a few votes, but the present Legislature is an exceptionally good one, and there have been, I think, enough exhibitions of the situation in our section to induce prompt and proper action by the two houses this winter.

Charlie Russell, whose industry helped to break up the Wheeling Standard, and who subsequently made considerable reputation as a historical novelist, lives here now, and he told me, yesterday, that he had a couple of brand new novels nearly ready for the press. The scene of one of them is laid in Wheeling, and the heroine, a fragile daughter of the southland, breaks one of her lower limbs in the second chapter. This naturally brings about an estrangement, but mutual explanations and corrections follow, and what might have been a fatal separation glides peacefully into a happy and enduring union. WHOLESALE SHOOTING BY A LUNATIC.

CHICAGO, Sept. 2.—John C. Neal, a crazy stranger, last night about 1 o'clock, arose from bed in a lodging house at 353 Clark street, and suddenly placed a revolver to the head of another inmate of the room, David Fagin, and fired. He then darted down stairs to the office, and, with an Indian war whoop, shot the only occupant, an old Swede man named Springcard, in the back, then took a running jump out of the window and struck squarely on his feet and started down Clark street on a dead run, firing as he ran, and killing Henry Johnson, a negro, who attempted to stop him. Reaching Polk street, he fired at close range at Thomas Flynn, a railroad flagman, and William Wolf, the depot watchman, who were sitting together. Running still farther, he snapped his revolver twice at a policeman, who clubbed the excited lunatic, and after a violent struggle got him to the armory. The wounds of Wolf, Springcard and Johnson are serious, and may prove fatal. The lunatic claims to have been a grocer in Troy, N.Y.

CHICAGO, Sept. 2.—Fire broke out at 10 o'clock to night in the building on southeast corner of Lake and Franklin streets, No. 37 to 45, Franklin, which burned two houses before fully mastered. The building is in the form of an L and fronts on both streets. The first floor and basement, occupied by Durrand Bros. & Co., grocers, who carried a very heavy stock, estimated to be nearly $200,000 in value. It was badly damaged by water. M., November 9.—This town, from which so much was once expected by those who had invested their ducats in town lots here, seems to have relapsed into a chronic state of dullness—only occasionally relieved by the visits of the festive cowboy, and even these have become rather spiritless since the wiping out of one of their number by Sheriff Tucker not long since.

A most atrocious crime was committed Saturday night at Kingston, a small hamlet in DeSoto parish, about twelve miles northeast of Mansfield. MANSFIELD, July 19, 1881.

EDITOR TIMES.—Mr. M. J. Scott, a merchant and citizen of this parish, doing business at Kingston, was foully murdered on Saturday night, about 9 o'clock. He was at the time returning to the store from his boarding house, some two or three hundred yards distant with a lantern in his hand; was waylaid and shot in the back of the head, the shot entirely tearing away the back portion of the head, just as he was passing from the enclosure of his boarding-house. The news of this tragic event which reached us Sunday morning, was a great shock to the community. Mr. Scott was one of our best citizens and was not known to have an enemy in the world.

Sheriff Sample, with his usual energy and promptness, upon receipt of the first tidings, repaired to the scene of the tragedy and will probe the matter to the bottom, if it can be done. He sent to jail on Monday two negroes suspicioned of the crime. Last night the keys of the jail were forced from the jailor by some thirty or forty men presumed to reside in the vicinity of Kingston, and one of the prisoners, suspected, Wash Allen by name, was taken out, carried back to Kingston and hung there about daylight this morning. These men are generally known to be men of coolness and deliberation, and men who would not act hastily and without sufficient evidence. Allen is said to have confessed the crime before the hanging. The action of these gentlemen, so far as we have been able to learn, is approved in toto by the citizens of mansfield. It is idle to talk or think of the slow process of the law when so great a crime has been committed. Robbery was the incentive to the murder. All facts point to this conclusion. In this the murderer failed entirely. Very truly, JOSEPH JONES.

THE SCOTT MURDER.
A Full Confession Made by Wash Allen, Whose Case, Was Dispos ed of by Judge Lynch
Shreveport Times.

Yesterday afternoon, Mr. McDeavreaux, driver of the Mansfield stage, brought information to the effect that the negro, Wash Allen, who was taken from the Mansfield jail Monday night by 30 or 40 masked men and hung at Kingston, the particulars of which were given yesterday by the Times, made a clean breast of the whole affair, implicating four or five others, and informed the crowd where the gun with which he committed the terrible deed could be found and detailed the manner in which the whole affair was conducted.

The parties—all negroes—implicated by Allen were arrested Tuesday and taken to Manfield and confined in the parish jail.

The gun was found at the very spot where Allen said he had secreted it, and on the locks were found blood and hair of the murdered man. He stated that the killing of Mr. Scott was a prearranged affair and the four or five others, whom he implicated, stood guard while he did the shooting, and after he had fired the fatal shot, to make death doubly sure, he approached the prostrate form of Mr. Scott and dealt him several heavy blows with the gun, crushing in the forehead.

Minden Democrat: Saturday night as Mr. M. Judd Scott, of Kingston, a little place a few miles north of Mansfield, was going from the house where he boarded, to his store, a distance of about 250 yards, he was shot and instantly killed. The murder was not found out until next morning when his body was found riddled with buckshot. The murderers rifled his pockets, went to his store and took fifty or sixty dollars that was in the drawer, but were unable to get the safe open. A Negro named Wash Allen was suspicioned as being one of the parties. His house was searched, resulting in the finding of a watch and several articles of clothing belonging to Mr. Scott; also a pair of pants that the murderer wore the previous day which were stained with blood. He was taken to Mansfield and incarcerated. At night an armed body of men rode into town and aroused the deputy Sheriff, informing him that they had a prisoner they wished to lock up. The Sheriff went to the jail, when they immediately overpowered and took the key from him. They then unlocked the cell, took out the Negro and went off with him. The next morning he was found hanging to a limb a few yards from where the crime was committed. Other parties are implicated. Investigation in progress.

A colored man named Philip Jackson was shot and mortally wounded while sitting in front of the house of Dave Barnhill, in the Lake country. Claiborne Guardian: The cotton worm appeared on Red river much earlier than usual this year, but the chrysalis was destroyed by the heat or by some insect or bird. A large planter near Shreveport told the writer that he found numbers so destroyed. His conclusion was that no serious damage would be done the crop. Deputy Sheriff, I. N. Glover, captured Sunday morning, two miles below Vienna, Charlie Johnson and Sarah Coleman, who had murdered Squire Coleman near Shreveport, a short time since. Mr. Glover left with the prisoners for Shreveport. John Cupp of this parish was robbed last Thursday Thursday night of $1300. Mr. Cupp was away from home at the time. The house was entered and the money taken out, showing that the robbery must have been committed by some person familiar with the house.
wash-allen-shreveport-1881-07-19.A24: THE HORRORS OF. LYNCH LAW.—The negro Wash Allen, who was lynched for the murder of Mr. M. J. Scott at Kingston, was swung up sixteen or eighteen times to extort a confession from him. When taken down he told a disconnected story and implicated other negroes, who clearly proved an alibi. Several times the hardened wretch laughed in the face of the party after he was let down, and never begged for mercy, though he asked to be shot. Sheriff Sample says he was one of the most intractable prisoners he ever had in charge.—Shreveport (La.) Times.
